rewritten_text:
I spent two years this way. Hundreds of days passed, one after another, bringing no outward changes, though a few changes slowly took place in my mind as I drifted toward death. I began to study more, to feel more deeply the thoughts others expressed in books, to read history and lose my own identity among the multitude who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the sharpness of immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude, too, lost some of its attraction. Once again I longed for understanding. I never felt drawn to a crowd, but I wished for a single friend who would love me. Perhaps you will say that I was gradually becoming ready to return to society. I don't believe so. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure, so free from the influence of external circumstances, that in the world I would inevitably have been disappointed by the coarse concerns that constantly mix with even its best feelings. Believe me, I was less prepared then for companionship with other people than I had been before. When I left them, they had tormented me as illness or pain might: something outside the mind that irritated it and that I wanted to remove. Now, however, I would have sought understanding. I would have wanted to bind my soul to another person's, and so would have prepared abundant disappointment and suffering for myself. I was as delicate as the sensitive plant, all nerves. I wanted neither shared ambition nor help in acquiring wisdom, but gentle, mutual affection: smiles to lift my spirits and soft words to comfort me. I longed for one heart into which I could freely pour my complaints, where the heavenly goodness of the soil might bring blessed fruit from such poor seed. Yet where could I find it? The love at the heart of friendship is a tender spirit, seldom found unless two kind people have been joined since early youth or united by shared suffering and pursuits. It comes uninvited and unexpectedly to a chosen few. Like gentle dew, it settles on certain places and makes them fertile with every sweet plant, however barren they were before. But when pursued, it flees; it mocks the prayers of those who worship it. It gives itself, but will not be sought.

I understood all this and did not search for sympathy. Yet there on my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof with desolation all around, it came to me like a winter sunbeam, brightening the drifted snow while helping it melt. Alas, the sunlight fell on ruined fruit. I did not recover beneath its glow, for I was too utterly broken to feel its healing warmth.

But that same peaceful Saturday afternoon brought no laughter to the little town. The Harpers and Aunt Polly's family were being dressed in mourning amid deep grief and many tears. An unusual hush settled over the village, quiet though it generally was. People went about their business distractedly and spoke little, but sighed often. The children seemed weighed down by their Saturday holiday. They had no enthusiasm for their games and gradually stopped playing.

That afternoon, Becky Thatcher found herself wandering gloomily around the empty schoolyard. Nothing there offered any comfort. She said to herself:

‘Oh, if only I had that brass knob from the fireplace stand again! Now I haven't a single thing to remember him by.’ She swallowed a small sob.

After a while she stopped and murmured:

‘It happened right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't say it for anything in the world. But he's gone now. I'll never, never, never see him again.’

That thought overwhelmed her, and she wandered off with tears running down her cheeks. Soon a whole group of boys and girls, Tom's and Joe's playmates, came along. They stood peering over the picket fence, speaking solemnly about what Tom had done the last time they saw him and the little things Joe had said—things they could now plainly see were full of terrible warnings! Each child pointed out the exact place where the missing boys had stood, then added something like, ‘And I was standing just like this—exactly as I am now, and suppose you were him—I was that close. He smiled like this, and then a feeling came over me, something awful, you know. Of course I didn't realize what it meant then, but I understand now!’

Then they argued over who had been the last to see the dead boys alive. Many claimed that gloomy honour, presenting evidence their own accounts had more or less improved upon. When they finally settled who had seen the departed last and spoken the final words to them, those fortunate children assumed a kind of sacred importance. Everyone else stared at them with envy. One poor boy, having nothing else impressive to contribute, announced with fairly obvious pride in the memory:

‘Well, Tom Sawyer beat me up once.’

But that attempt at glory failed. Most of the boys could say the same, which made the honour far too common to count for much. The group slowly drifted away, still recalling their lost heroes in hushed, awed voices.

‘Starved you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean, Sir Simon—are you hungry? I've got a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?’

‘No, thank you. I never eat now. Still, it's very kind of you. You're much nicer than the rest of your dreadful, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ Virginia cried, stamping her foot. ‘You're the one who's rude, dreadful, and vulgar. And speaking of dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to touch up that absurd bloodstain in the library. First you took every red I had, including the vermilion, so I couldn't paint any more sunsets. Then you took my emerald green and chrome yellow. Eventually all I had left was indigo and Chinese white, and I could only paint moonlit scenes. They're always depressing to look at, and they're certainly not easy to paint. I didn't tell on you, although I was very annoyed. The whole thing was ridiculous anyway. Whoever heard of emerald-green blood?’

‘Well, really,’ the Ghost replied rather meekly, ‘what else could I do? Real blood is very hard to come by these days. Since your brother started the whole affair with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason not to use your paints. As for colour, that's always a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, for example—the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don't value that sort of thing.’

‘You don't know anything about it. The best thing you could do is emigrate and broaden your mind. My father would gladly pay your passage. There's a high import tax on spirits of every kind, but customs won't be a problem, since all the officials are Democrats. Once you're in New York, you're bound to be a great success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather, and far more for a family ghost.’

‘I don't think I'd like America.’

‘I suppose that's because we have no ruins or curiosities,’ Virginia said sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ the Ghost replied. ‘You have your navy and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I'll go and ask Papa to give the twins another week's holiday.’

‘Please don't leave, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I'm terribly lonely and unhappy, and I truly don't know what to do. I want to sleep, but I can't.’

‘That's absurd! All you have to do is get into bed and blow out the candle.’
